Female Gulf hake (Urophycis cirrata) reach a maximum recorded total length of 66 centimeters [Li = 66 centimeters], a value established from extensive trawl surveys conducted throughout the northern Gulf of Mexico. This ultimate size is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 2409 grams [Wwi = 2409 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required to attain such dimensions in a demersal gadiform inhabiting continental shelf waters. In contrast, the total length at which females first achieve puberty is considerably smaller, measured at 33 centimeters [Lp = 33 centimeters], a threshold that marks the onset of gametogenesis and the transition from a purely somatic growth phase to one that includes reproductive allocation. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 271 grams [Wwp = approximately 271 grams], indicating that females must accumulate roughly one-ninth of their ultimate body mass before reproductive maturation becomes physiologically feasible. This pronounced disparity between size at maturity and maximum size is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction while still permitting substantial post-pubertal growth, a pattern commonly observed in iteroparous marine teleosts that face moderate to high adult mortality rates.

At a stable water temperature of 11.5 °C [T = 11.5 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval from egg fertilisation to larval eclosion, has been estimated at 13.5 days [ab = 13.5 days]. This relatively brief incubation period, characteristic of pelagic eggs spawned in warm-temperate waters, is facilitated by the rapid cleavage and gastrulation rates typical of small, yolk-dependent teleost embryos. The fertilised ovum, a transparent, pelagic egg measuring approximately 0.6 millimeters in diameter, develops quickly through the blastula and gastrula stages before hatching enzyme secretion triggers chorion rupture and the emergence of a yolk-sac larva. The wet weight at birth for these newly hatched prolarvae is exceedingly low, calculated at 0.00011 grams per individual [Wwb = 0.00011 grams per individual], a value that underscores the minimal maternal investment per offspring in a species that produces large numbers of small, planktonic larvae. This endotrophic, non-feeding stage persists until mouth opening and retinal differentiation permit the onset of exogenous feeding, at which point the larvae must successfully capture their first prey to avoid the point of no return.

Under identical thermal conditions of 11.5 °C [T = 11.5 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for Gulf hake in the wild has been documented at 5110 days [am = 5110 days], equivalent to approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years]. This lifespan is comparatively extended for a gadiform of its moderate body size, suggesting that adult mortality rates in this species are relatively low once individuals have recruited to the benthic juvenile stage following larval metamorphosis and settlement. The transition from a pelagic larval phase to a demersal, benthic juvenile existence represents a critical bottleneck, with mortality during this period likely exerting strong selective pressure on growth rate and developmental timing. Post-settlement juveniles then enter a prolonged sub-adult phase during which they accumulate the body mass necessary to achieve the pubertal threshold. The combination of a late lifespan and a moderate size at puberty implies a life-history strategy that balances the advantages of extended reproductive tenure against the risks of delayed maturation, a trade-off that is particularly relevant for species inhabiting variable shelf environments where recruitment success may be highly episodic.

The maximum daily reproduction rate for female Gulf hake, derived from fecundity estimates for the congeneric species Urophycis tenuis and scaled to the body size of Urophycis cirrata, has been inferred from the annual reproductive output at 11.5 °C [T = 11.5 °C]. Field evidence indicates that mature females release approximately 4660 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 4660 eggs per spawning event], and spawning occurs daily during the peak season [F_R_i = spawning occurs daily during the peak season], yielding a daily reproduction rate of 4660 eggs per day [Ri = 4660 eggs per day]. This high fecundity is achieved through the production of multiple batches of pelagic eggs over an extended spawning period, with a single female capable of releasing nearly 1.7 million eggs over the course of a full annual cycle. The strategy of producing numerous small, yolk-laden eggs with a correspondingly brief embryonic development time is typical of marine teleosts that rely on high larval abundance to overcome immense planktonic mortality. These demersal spawning adults exhibit iteroparous reproduction, breeding repeatedly over their fourteen-year lifespan (14 years) [am = 14 years] and thereby distributing reproductive effort across multiple years to buffer against interannual variability in larval survival conditions at a temperature of 11.5 °C [T = 11.5 °C].

Comparative analysis of life-history traits among western Atlantic phycid hakes reveals that Gulf hake exhibits a particularly pronounced allometric relationship between length and mass, with the ultimate wet weight of 2409 grams [Wwi = 2409 grams] attained at the asymptotic length of 66 centimeters [Li = 66 centimeters]. This length-mass scaling, derived from field-collected specimens ranging from recently metamorphosed juveniles to reproductively active adults, demonstrates that females continue to add substantial somatic tissue well after the onset of sexual maturity. The wet weight at puberty of 271 grams [Wwp = 271 grams] represents only about eleven percent of the ultimate body mass, indicating that gonadal recrudescence begins at a relatively early stage of somatic development compared to many other demersal gadiforms. At the other extreme of the size spectrum, the minuscule wet weight at birth of 0.00011 grams per individual [Wwb = 0.00011 grams per individual] highlights the enormous disparity between neonatal and adult mass, a ratio exceeding twenty million to one that is characteristic of teleosts with pelagic eggs and planktonic larvae. Individual larvae that survive the critical transition to exogenous feeding and subsequently recruit to the benthic juvenile stage must undergo a period of rapid mass gain, sustained by progressively increasing prey detection capacity and swim bladder inflation, before reaching the 33-centimeter pubertal threshold.
